'''''Melaleuca citrina''''', the '''common red bottlebrush''', '''crimson bottlebrush''', or '''lemon bottlebrush''',<ref name=pfaf>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon citrinus''|url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Callistemon+citrinus|publisher=Plants for a Future|accessdate=12 June 2015}}</ref> is a plant in the myrtle [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Myrtaceae]], and is [[Endemism|endemic]] to eastern Australia. Some Australian state herbaria continue to use the name ''Callistemon citrinus''.<ref name=Udovicic>{{cite journal|last1=Udovicic|first1=Frank|last2=Spencer|first2=Roger|title=New combinations in ''Callistemon'' (Myrtaceae)|journal=Muelleria|date=2012|volume=30|issue=1|pages=23–25|doi=10.5962/p.292240 |s2cid=251007557 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/59605029#page/25/mode/1up|accessdate=25 August 2021|doi-access=free}}</ref> It is a hardy and adaptable species, common in its natural habitat. It is widely cultivated, not only in Australia. It was one of the first Australian plants to be grown outside the country, having been taken to England in 1770 by [[Joseph Banks]]. Its showy red flower spikes, present over most of the year in an ideal situation, account for its popularity.

==Description==
''Melaleuca citrina'' is a shrub that lives for approximately ten years<ref>https://www.nparks.gov.sg/florafaunaweb/flora/2/7/2772 Growth Form: A large shrub to small tree, up to about 7-8m tall, with a life span of slightly over a decade in its place of origin.</ref> and grows to {{convert|5|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} tall but more usually in the range {{convert|1-3|m|ft|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} high and wide. It has hard, fibrous or papery bark and its young growth is usually covered with soft, silky hairs. Its leaves are arranged alternately and are {{convert|26-99|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|4-25|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide, hard, flat, narrow egg-shaped with the narrower end near the base and with a pointed but not sharp end. There are between 7 and 26 branching veins clearly visible on both sides of the leaves and a large number of distinct oil glands visible on both surfaces of the leaves.<ref name=Brophy>{{cite book|last1=Brophy|first1=Joseph J.|last2=Craven|first2=Lyndley A.|last3=Doran|first3=John C.|title=Melaleucas : their botany, essential oils and uses|date=2013|publisher=Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research|location=Canberra|isbn=9781922137517|page=119}}</ref><ref name=plantnet>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon citrinus''|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Callistemon~citrinus|publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney: PlantNet|accessdate=12 June 2015}}</ref>

The flowers are red and arranged in spikes on the ends of branches that continue to grow after flowering and sometimes also in the upper leaf axils. The spikes are up to {{convert|45-70|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} in diameter and {{convert|60-100|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long with up to 80 individual flowers. The petals are {{convert|3.9-5.8|mm|in|sigfig=2|abbr=on}} long and fall off as the flower ages. There are 30 to 45 [[stamen]]s in each flower, with their "stalks" (the filaments) red and "tips" (the anthers) purple. Flowering occurs in most months of the year but mainly in November and December. Flowering is followed by fruit that are woody, cup-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]]s, {{convert|4.4-7|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} long and about {{convert|7|mm|in|sigfig=1|abbr=on}} wide in cylindrical clusters along the stem. The fruiting capsules remain unopened until the plant, or the part bearing them dies.<ref name="Brophy" /><ref name="plantnet" />

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Melaleuca citrina'' was first formally described in 1802 by the French botanist [[Georges Louis Marie Dumont de Courset]] in ''[[Le Botaniste Cultivateur]]''.<ref name=APNI(2)>{{cite web|title=''Melaleuca citrina''|url=  https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/509658|publisher=APNI|accessdate=12 June 2015}}</ref> The species had previously been known as ''Metrosideros citrina'', in turn named by [[William Curtis]] in the ''[[Botanical Magazine]]'' in 1794, based on a flowering plant growing at [[Thomas Dawson, 1st Viscount Cremorne|Lord Cremorne]]'s estate. That plant had grown from a root collected in 1770 at [[Botany Bay]] by [[Joseph Banks]] during the [[first voyage of James Cook]] to Australia. Curtis noted that the leaves "when bruised give forth an agreeable fragrance."<ref name=Curtis>{{cite book|last1=Curtis|first1=William|title=The Botanical Magazine (Volume 8)|date=1794|location=London|page=260|edition=1|url=http://www.gutenberg.org/files/24670/24670-h/24670-h.htm#Metrosideros_Citrina_Harsh-Leavd_Metrosideros|accessdate=12 June 2015}}</ref><ref name=APNI(3)>{{cite web|title=''Metrosideros citrina''|url=  https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/541790|publisher=APNI|accessdate=12 June 2015}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''citrina'') alludes to the similarity of the aromatic property of leaves of this species and those of [[citrus]] plants.<ref name="Brophy" />

''Callistemon citrinus'' is regarded as a synonym of ''Melaleuca citrina'' by [[Plants of the World Online]].<ref name ="POWO" />

==Distribution and habitat==
''Melaleuca citrina'' occurs in near coastal areas of New South Wales, including the [[Blue Mountains (New South Wales)|Blue Mountains]] and extends as far west as the Central Western Slopes.<ref name="plantnet" /> It also occurs in the east coast areas of Victoria<ref name="Brophy" /> and grows in swamps and along creeks and rivers.<ref name="plantnet" />

==Ecology==
Birds have been observed using the species as a source of food. Those seeking nectar from the flowers include [[eastern spinebill]]s, [[New Holland honeyeater]]s, [[noisy miner]]s, [[red wattlebird]]s and [[silvereye]]s, while [[crimson rosella]]s eat the seeds.<ref name=Lepschi>{{cite journal|author=Lepschi, B.J.|title=Food of some birds in eastern New South Wales"Additions to Barker & Vestjens|journal=Emu|volume=93|pages=195–199|year=1993|url=http://www.publish.csiro.au/?act=view_file&file_id=MU9930195.pdf|doi=10.1071/MU9930195|issue=3}}</ref>

==Uses==
===Agriculture===
The herbicide [[Mesotrione]] was developed as a synthetic analogue of [[leptospermone]], a natural herbicide produced by the roots of ''Callistemon citrinus''.<ref name=cornes>{{cite web|last1=Cornes|first1=Derek|title=Fourth World Congress on Allelopathy |url=http://www.regional.org.au/au/allelopathy/2005/2/7/2636_cornesd.htm|publisher=The Regional Institute Ltd.|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref>

===Honey production===
Usefully, the plant blooms extendedly for most of the year, from March to October.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=XLFQEAAAQBAJ&dq=%22tecoma+stans%22%2B%22honey%22&pg=SA2-PA29 Honey: A Miraculous Product of Nature.]</ref>

===Horticulture===
''M. citrina'', as ''Callistemon citrinus''  had become established in cultivation in England by 1794 when flowering plants that were more than five years old had been observed at both [[Kew Gardens]] and [[Syon House]] and younger plants had become available in nurseries.<ref name="Curtis" /> It is widely cultivated, often as ''Callistemon citrinus'' and sometimes as ''Callistemon lanceolatus''. It is easily propagated from seed or [[Cutting (plant)|cuttings]] and grows in most soils, preferring a sunny location. It is frost hardy and responds well to watering and the application of fertiliser but is tolerant of drought and frost.<ref name="pfaf" /><ref name=ANPSA>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon citrinus''|url=http://anpsa.org.au/c-cit.html|publisher=Australian Native Plants Society Australia|accessdate=20 July 2015}}</ref><ref name=anbg>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon citrinus''|url=https://www.anbg.gov.au/gnp/gnp2/callistemon-citrinus.html|publisher=Australian National Botanic Garden|accessdate=12 June 2015}}</ref>

A number of cultivars have been developed (as cultivars of ''Callistemon citrinus'') including:<ref name=ACRA>{{cite web|title=List of Registered Cultivars derived from Australian native flora|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/acra-list-2009.html|publisher=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority Inc.|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref>

* 'Demesne Rowena' - A cross between 'Splendens' and 'White Anzac' growing to 1.5 x 1.5 metres. The flowers are red upon opening, fading to deep pink.<ref name=ACRA(1)>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon'' 'Demesne Rowena' |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc288.html|publisher=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref>
* 'Firebrand', a seedling of uncertain origin first planted at Austraflora Nursery in 1973. Plants are about 60 cm high and 2.5 metres wide and have deep crimson-pink flowers.<ref name=ACRA(2)>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon'' 'Firebrand'|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc191.html|publisher=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref>
* [[Callistemon 'Splendens'|'Splendens']], a form with a compact and rounded habit, growing to about 2 metres high and wide. In Australia, it is sold under the trade name "Endeavour".<ref name=ACRA(3)>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon'' 'Splendens'|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc459.html|publisher=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref> In the UK it has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/99397/Callistemon-citrinus-Splendens/Details | title = ''Callistemon citrinus'' 'Splendens' | website = www.rhs.org | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 12 April 2020}}</ref> 
* 'White Anzac', a low, spreading white-flowering form selected from a natural population in New South Wales.<ref name=ACRA(4)>{{cite web|title=''Callistemon'' 'White Anzac'|url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/acra/descriptions/acc239.html|publisher=Australian Cultivar Registration Authority|accessdate=18 July 2015}}</ref>
